files.name: SessionStore.cs

notes.9: Decodes the base64 cookie value into raw bytes.
notes.10: Wraps those bytes in a readable stream.
notes.11: Creates a BinaryFormatter — a serializer that can reconstruct arbitrary .NET types.
notes.12: Reads the stream, rebuilding whatever object graph it describes, then casts the result to SessionState.
notes.19: Save() serializes a SessionState back into the binary format.
notes.20: Returns it base64-encoded for use as a cookie.

options.label: An attacker can edit the base64 to change their own `role` field to admin
options.whyWrong: Field tampering is possible but minor next to the real problem — the payload need not be a SessionState at all.

options.label: The cast on line 12 throws for an unexpected type, letting an attacker crash the app
options.whyWrong: A crash is the least of it, and the cast runs only AFTER deserialization has already executed attacker code.

options.label: `Deserialize` instantiates whatever types the stream names and runs their callbacks, so a crafted cookie executes a gadget chain
Validate the object's type after deserializing
options.whyWrong: Too late: BinaryFormatter already instantiated the attacker's gadget chain during Deserialize. The cast/type check runs after code has executed.

options.label: Replace BinaryFormatter with a data-only serializer (e.g. System.Text.Json)
Encrypt the cookie value
options.whyWrong: Encryption/signing stops tampering by outsiders, but the format is still BinaryFormatter; if a key leaks or the data is ever attacker-influenced, the gadget problem remains. The dangerous sink is the formatter itself.

options.label: Wrap Deserialize in a try/catch and return a default session
options.whyWrong: A gadget chain executes its payload during deserialization and may complete without throwing. Catching exceptions does not prevent the code execution.

source.attribution: SourceReadle original (BinaryFormatter RCE pattern; see Microsoft BinaryFormatter security guide)

training.exploit: Use a tool like ysoserial.net to generate a `TypeConfuseDelegate` gadget-chain payload that runs `calc`/`id`, base64-encode it, and send it as the session cookie. When `Load` calls `Deserialize`, the chain fires during object reconstruction and the command runs on the server — remote code execution from an unauthenticated cookie.

hints.line: The sink is the single call that turns bytes back into a live object.
hints.why: Does the cast on line 12 happen before or after the object is built?
hints.fix: Use a serializer that only reads data into a known type.

writeup.summary: `BinaryFormatter.Deserialize` reconstructs whatever types the serialized stream names and invokes their callbacks, so a crafted cookie can drive a 'gadget chain' (e.g. via `TypeConfuseDelegate`) to run arbitrary code the moment it is deserialized — before any cast or validation. Because the input is a user-controlled cookie, this is remote code execution. Microsoft has deprecated BinaryFormatter for exactly this reason. The fix is to stop using it: a data-only serializer like System.Text.Json reads fields into a known type and never instantiates arbitrary types or runs their callbacks.
